summary: A directory compiled by the Network Information Center of how to get accounts at various ARPANET sites, issued after many requests. For each site it lists an address, contacts and what kinds of accounts are available. Corrections were to be sent to the NIC for the next Resource Notebook.

plainLanguage.summary: A phone-book-style list showing whom to contact at each network computer site to get an account.

subtitle: A directory of how to open an account at ARPANET sites in 1973.

tldr.problem: Network users needed to know which sites offered accounts and how to contact them to set one up.
tldr.mechanism: The Network Information Center compiled a directory listing each ARPANET site with its address, contact names and phone numbers, and what kinds of accounts were available (experimental, paid, file storage, etc.).
tldr.outcome: A simple reference document to help researchers and engineers find compute resources. The RFC invited corrections for the next edition of the Resource Notebook.

facts.label: Purpose
facts.value: Directory of account availability at ARPANET sites

today: RFC 518 is a snapshot of the ARPANET's early administrative landscape in 1973, showing which sites were willing to share resources with network users and on what terms. It was explicitly issued as a preliminary version, with plans to incorporate corrections and updates into the next Resource Notebook. As a historical administrative directory specific to that time, it has not been obsoleted or updated in the RFC series.

sections.title: The Account Directory
sections.content:
RFC 518 is a directory compiled by the Network Information Center in response to repeated requests for information on opening accounts at ARPANET sites. For each participating site, it lists a mailing address, the names and phone numbers of contacts, and what kinds of accounts were available.

The RFC was issued after it became clear that many researchers did not know whom to contact or what was available. Sites had different policies: some offered experimental accounts with no cost, some sold computer time, some restricted file storage, and others had different terms.
sections.plainLanguage: When people wanted to use computers on the network, they didn't always know which site had what they needed or who to call. This list gave them the answers.

sections.title: Sites and Services
sections.content:
The RFC lists sites including AMES-67, BBN-TNEX, CASE-10, CMU-10A, CCA, Harvard, MIT Lincoln Lab, and others, each with address and contact details. For example, BBN TENEX required a purchase order to open a paid account, while experimental use could be arranged with a contact. Harvard and Case Western offered limited experimental accounts, and some sites that sold computer time had varying policies.

Some sites offered file storage with accounts; others did not. The directory was designed as a practical resource for researchers on the network who needed to know where to get access to computing power.
sections.plainLanguage: Different sites had different rules. Some let you try for free, some charged money, and some didn't have space for your files.

sections.title: A Preliminary Directory
sections.content: The RFC was issued as an administrative reference in response to direct requests from network users. The authors recognized that the information would change as the network evolved and invited corrections and updates from the community. The document was designed to feed into the next edition of the NIC Resource Notebook.
sections.plainLanguage: This was a living document; the authors knew it would get outdated and asked people to send in changes.
